summary: LunarSight is a tool for engineers to iterate their design and mission planning, specifcally targeting startups. The central idea is a vehicle model on top of a physics engine to create a search space containing both engineering and mission parameters. We used ephemeris data and LOLA terrain mapping to generate 360 degree horizons at any point in the southern hemisphere and a mission optimizer for vehicle and mission parameters. We envision this tool being used by startups to build their own vehicle models to optimize their designs and help them reach the moon.
details:
Project Description: 

Overview: 

LunarSight is a lunar environmental and vehicle simulation tool that aims to bridge the gap between lunar mission planning and vehicle design. Engineering design philosophies such as Agile development and Rapid Prototype prioritizes building working models early and making continuous improvements. To promote this kind of engineering and the fast development in startups, this project enables these kind of developments by building a parameter search space in both engineering and mission design using four components: 

  1. Physics Backend 
  2. Vehicle Model 
  3. Parameter Optimizer 
  4. Frontend

The goal of this project is to provide a rigorously tested physics simulation engine that startups and other builders alike can build upon to explore both different vehicles and mission parameters. 

Components: 

Physics Backend

The heart of LunarSight is a physics backend that computes terrain horizons: the 360° skyline seen from any point in the lunar south polar region (86.7–90°S). Horizons are traced along 1,440 directions out to 200 km over NASA LOLA terrain (5 m near the landing sites, 40 m regionally), separately from the solar-mast and antenna heights. Each hour, the Sun’s and Earth’s positions (JPL DE421 ephemeris via NASA SPICE) are compared with the horizon to decide whether there is direct line of sight. From that come the key metrics: solar access, longest darkness, Earth visibility and longest Earth blackout, which are then checked against mission limits.

Because everything rests on these horizons and positions, both were validated against independent NASA and JPL references:

  1. Sun and Earth positions vs JPL Horizons. Horizons uses an independent ephemeris (DE441). We compared 16 cases: Sun and Earth, two south-polar locations (89.5°S and 85°S), 2027–2039. The worst difference was 0.00003° against a tolerance of 0.01°.
  2. Sunlight and Earth visibility vs NASA’s published south-pole maps [1, 2]. At 100 random points (87–90°S), the correlation was r = 0.991 (sunlight) and 0.993 (Earth), the mean offset ≤ 0.4 percentage points, and the RMS 1.7–2.5 percentage points. All met pre-set tolerances (±3 pp mean, ≤ 8 pp RMS, r ≥ 0.90).

Our model vs NASA’s published south-pole maps, at 100 random points (87–90°S). Each dot is one location. The horizontal axis is NASA’s published average visibility [1, 2]; the vertical axis is our model’s value for the same location, from 40 m terrain sampled hourly over 2026–2040. Both measure the percentage of time that any part of the body’s disk is above the terrain horizon. 

Vehicle Model

LunarSight currently models the lander as two independent observers, a solar mast and an antenna (each 0–20 m above the ground), each with its own 360° terrain horizon. This lets teams see exactly how instrument height affects sunlight and Earth line of sight, and find the minimum height that meets their mission limits. This vehicle definition is meant to be modified for greater fidelity to assess how vehicle design impacts mission and vice-versa. 

Parameter Optimizer

Whenever a proposed trajectory fails to satisfy solar access or line-of-sight communication thresholds, the Parameter Optimizer pinpoints the minimal parameter adjustment needed to restore viability. It screens three distinct pathways: altering instrument heights by calculating the lowest necessary elevation in 0.5 m increments up to 20 m; adjusting mission timing by identifying the closest valid launch window within a ±60-day window; and re-siting the landing target across 80 prospective locations within an 800 m radius, returning both the closest and highest-performing viable coordinates. Each proposed adjustment is validated through the core physics engine to guarantee exact repeatability. For instance, a 14-day surface deployment at Connecting Ridge in December 2030 initially proved unfeasible due to a 71-hour blackout period; the optimizer demonstrated viability could be achieved by elevating the solar mast from 6 m to 8 m, shifting the timeline forward by 7.9 days, or relocating the site by 200 m. A comprehensive search execution requires approximately 13 seconds. Upcoming iterations will evaluate multi-parameter trade spaces weighted by system complexity, integrate surface slope and hazard constraints into site selection, and incorporate power storage models to optimize overall system survivability rather than simple shadow avoidance.

Frontend

The frontend of LunarSight is developed using React functional components written in TypeScript, with Vite used for development and production builds. It communicates with a FastAPI back-end through HTTP requests using a defined JSON interface. The frontend retrieves the available site catalogue from the backend and submits user defined mission parameters, such as landing site coordinates, for analysis. The backend performs the necessary calculations and returns the structured JSON results containing terrain horizon profiles, Sun and Earth visibility, and mission feasibility metrics. The frontend then processes these results and presents them through interactive visualizations, allowing users to evaluate and compare potential landing sites.

LunarSight has three main views built-in: Lunar Map for choosing a waypoint, Horizon Analysis for understanding conditions, and Site Rankings for comparing options. The selected site, mission and vehicle parameters settings carry across views. 

The Lunar map provides an interface for selecting potential landing sites within the lunar south pole region. The selection can be done either by manually specifying longitude and latitude or can be entered in using the mission design tab. To convert between the lunar geographical coordinate system and the two dimensional map representation, the frontend implements a south polar stereographic projection. This allows the coordinates to be transformed into positions on the map while keeping a record of the lunar coordinates for the backend analysis. 

To maintain responsiveness when navigating high resolution imagery, the frontend uses a tiled image loading system. High resolution imagery, from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), can be requested as needed. The frontend determines the appropriate image resolution based on the map zoom level and display pixel density, requesting only the tiles necessary for the current view. 

The Horizon Analysis view converts the backend’s numerical results into an interactive visualization of the terrain surrounding the selected landing site. A HTML canvas based chart, scaled to the display’s pixel density, renders the 360-degree terrain horizon profile alongside the apparent trajectories on the Sun and the Earth. Users can adjust the displayed azimuth range to inspect specific sections of the surrounding terrain. The chart also accounts for wraparound, ensuring that trajectories cross the 0-degree and 360-degree boundary are displayed continuously. 

A key feature of the frontend is its ability to support the iterative mission and vehicle design. Users can modify parameters sich as the solar mast height and rerun the analysis to assess how the change influences site suitability. The frontend preserves the previous configuration as a baseline and overlays the corresponding horizon profiles while displaying changes in relevant mission metrics. This enables users to directly compare configurations and identify how adjustments to the vehicle affect the mission feasibility. 

Limitations:

The Sun and Earth are treated as points at their centres, and Earth visibility is a geometric line of sight rather than a full communications link. Solar access measures sunlight, not power generated, and analyses use hourly time steps. About 90% of the 5 m terrain is interpolated between altimeter tracks, and coverage currently extends to 86.7°S. 

Future Work: 

LunarSight delivers rapid, verified data on solar access, Earth visibility, and operational timelines for south-polar targets to commercial space ventures, including lander, rover, power, and communications engineers, while pinpointing optimal parameter adjustments for mission success. Through a flexible JSON interface and API, organizations can seamlessly integrate custom lander and rover configurations into the backend engine. Future additions to the software architecture will expand functionality to encompass integrated power and link-budget simulations, worldwide terrain support, environmental uncertainty margins, and automated landing site risk analysis.

Tools: 

We used Claude (Anthropic), via Claude Code, as an AI coding assistant. It implemented much of the backend, the planning tools and parts of the frontend, and drafted documentation. Our team set the requirements and design decisions, reviewed and approved each physics component against documented evidence, and validated the results against NASA and JPL references. 

References:

[2] LRO LOLA Team (2016). Average solar and Earth visibility maps, 85–90°S, 60 m/pixel (AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608, AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608_EARTH). NASA Planetary Data System, LOLA RDR extras: https://imbrium.mit.edu/EXTRAS/ILLUMINATION/
